nameStory: The Glassy Lyonsia gets its name from its remarkably translucent shell that looks almost like frosted glass when held up to the light. The genus name 'Lyonsia' honors Georges Lyons, a 19th-century French naturalist who studied marine mollusks. When you find one of these delicate clams on the beach, you'll immediately understand why 'glassy' made it into the common name!
description: The Glassy Lyonsia is a small, delicate clam with thin, translucent shells that have an almost glass-like quality. These little bivalves typically measure only about half an inch to three-quarters of an inch across, making them easy to overlook among beach debris. Their shells are somewhat oval-shaped and appear whitish or pale yellow, with a smooth, glossy surface that feels fragile to the touch. Unlike many clams, their shells don't close tightly together, leaving small gaps even when the clam tries to shut completely.

idTips.label: Translucent Shell
idTips.description: Hold the shell up to sunlight or a bright light - you can actually see through it like frosted glass, with a pearly, opalescent quality that shimmers

idTips.label: Gaping Shell
idTips.description: Even when closed, the shells don't seal completely shut and leave noticeable gaps at the edges, unlike most clams that clamp tight

idTips.label: Fragile Texture
idTips.description: The shells feel paper-thin and delicate in your hands, almost brittle, and may crack easily with gentle pressure

idTips.label: Small Size
idTips.description: Typically smaller than your thumbnail, rarely exceeding three-quarters of an inch in length

idTips.label: Smooth Surface
idTips.description: Shell surface feels glassy-smooth with no ridges or bumps, often with a slight pearly sheen that catches light

idTips.label: Pale Coloration
idTips.description: Whitish to pale yellow color, sometimes with faint pinkish or greenish tints, but never dark or heavily patterned

habitat: Look for Glassy Lyonsia shells washed up on sandy and muddy beaches throughout New England's coastline, particularly in protected bays and estuaries. Living clams burrow in soft sediments in shallow coastal waters, often in areas with eelgrass beds. You're most likely to find empty shells along the wrack line after storms or high tides bring them ashore.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after spring storms, appearing bright and translucent. Living clams become more active in warming waters.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for finding shells on beaches during regular beachcombing. Living clams are most active in the warmer waters.
seasonality.fall: Storm activity brings more shells to shore. Look for recently deposited specimens in fresh wrack lines after nor'easters.
seasonality.winter: Shells become more weathered and brittle. Living clams retreat deeper into sediment during coldest months.

funFact: Despite their incredibly fragile appearance, Glassy Lyonsia clams are actually filter-feeders that can pump and filter several times their body volume in seawater every hour, making them tiny but mighty water purifiers in coastal ecosystems!
confusionNotes: Most commonly confused with small quahog or littleneck clam juveniles, but the Glassy Lyonsia's translucent, gaping shell is the dead giveaway - hold it up to light and remember 'glassy gaps' versus the opaque, tightly-closing shells of other small clams.
compareHints: Since Glassy Lyonsia is the only species in its genus found in New England waters, compare it to other small, thin-shelled clams like the Fragile Atlantic Macoma. The Lyonsia's translucent, glass-like quality and permanently gaping shell distinguish it from Macomas, which have opaque white shells that close more completely. The Lyonsia also lacks the slight bend or twist that characterizes Macoma shells.
